title: The Matter of the Sacred Bull
body: Sub-Inspector Diwan Chand petitions, with immense dignity, that a Brahminy bull — holy, enormous, and wholly above the law — has for the third time eaten the marigolds he had grown for the flower show. He requests that the bull be, in his words, ‘officially discouraged.’

choices.label: Solemnly issue a written order that the bull be kept off official flowerbeds.
choices.outcome: The order is framed and hung in the police lines. The bull cannot read it. Everyone is nonetheless satisfied that Something Has Been Done.

choices.label: Have the bull quietly relocated to a distant village.
choices.outcome: The village it is relocated to takes the arrival of a holy bull as an omen, and a deputation arrives within the week to ask what they have done to deserve it.

choices.label: Refuse to involve the district administration in bovine theology.
choices.outcome: Correct, dignified, and entirely useless. Diwan Chand's marigolds are eaten a fourth time. He does not forgive you, but he does respect you, which is worse.

title: The Billiards Subscription
body: An extraordinary meeting of the Chhota Nagra Club is convened over a proposal to raise the billiards subscription by four annas. Mrs. Fortescue-Vane is for. Major Prewitt is violently against. Both look to you, the new Magistrate, to settle a question that has already ended two friendships.

choices.label: Side with Mrs. Fortescue-Vane. One does not cross her.
choices.outcome: You are now, invisibly and permanently, Mrs. Fortescue-Vane's man. This is worth more than a knighthood and costs roughly the same in dignity.

choices.label: Side with Major Prewitt and the principle of the thing.
choices.outcome: The Major shakes your hand as though you have relieved Mafeking. Mrs. Fortescue-Vane says nothing at all, which is how you know.

choices.label: Propose a sub-committee to study the matter.
choices.outcome: You have discovered the single most powerful instrument of British administration: the postponement of a decision until everyone has forgotten why they cared.

title: The Revenue Is Short
body: A telegram from Commissioner Blyth-Curram, who communicates exclusively in telegrams and disappointment: REVENUE RETURNS CHHOTA NAGRA UNSATISFACTORY STOP EXPECT IMPROVEMENT STOP NO EXCUSES REGARDING RAINFALL WILL BE ENTERTAINED STOP. The rains, it should be said, have failed.

choices.label: Press the collection hard. Simla wants numbers.
choices.outcome: The numbers improve. So does the queue outside Lala Hukum Chand's door, as cultivators borrow at ruinous interest to pay a revenue the fields did not grow.

choices.label: Quietly grant remissions and massage the paperwork.
choices.outcome: You have committed the administrator's original sin: mercy off the books. If it is never discovered you are a good officer. If it is, you are a bad one. The difference is entirely a matter of discovery.

choices.label: Send Simla a magnificent report explaining the rainfall.
choices.outcome: Blyth-Curram replies: RAINFALL NOTED STOP REVENUE STILL SHORT STOP. You have learned that a telegram is not a conversation.

title: The Tiger of Rampur
body: Villagers from Rampur report a tiger that has taken two goats and a good deal of sleep. They ask the Magistrate-sahib, as tradition demands, to shoot it. You have fired a rifle four times in your life, twice by accident. The whole district is, however, watching to see whether the new sahib is a shikari or a clerk.

choices.label: Go out and shoot it yourself. It is expected.

ifTrue.outcome: By a miracle compounded of luck and a very close range, the tiger falls. You are, from this fortnight, a pukka sahib in the fullest sense. You are also never going to do that again.

ifFalse.outcome: Your nerves, already frayed, betray you. The tiger escapes; the story does not. A magistrate who cannot shoot straight is a magistrate the district has quietly stopped fearing.

choices.label: Send for a professional shikari from the next district.
choices.outcome: The tiger is dealt with, efficiently and by somebody else. Rampur is grateful and faintly disappointed. A sahib who sends for help is a useful sort of man, but not a legend.

choices.label: Declare it a matter for the Forest Department.
choices.outcome: Correct procedure. The Forest Department will attend to the tiger in the fullness of time, by which the tiger and everyone in Rampur understand: never.

title: The Rains Have Failed
body: There is no rain, and there will be no rain, and the district knows what that word means better than any word in the revenue code. Grain prices climb; the first families sell their cooking pots; a relief works could be opened, but relief works cost money the treasury does not have and Simla did not budget for.

choices.label: Open relief works at once and account for it later.
choices.outcome: Grain-for-labour on the roads and tanks. People do not starve, which no one will thank you for, because averted disasters leave no monument. The treasury, however, remembers.

choices.label: Wait for sanction from Simla before spending a rupee.
choices.outcome: You follow procedure exactly. Sanction arrives in six weeks, which is four weeks after it would have mattered. The files are impeccable. The district is not.

choices.label: Lean on Lala Hukum Chand to release grain on credit.
choices.outcome: The grain flows, at the Lala's interest and on the Lala's terms, and the district's debt to him deepens by a generation. You have solved this famine with a promise the next one will have to keep.

title: The Commissioner Inspects
body: Commissioner Blyth-Curram descends upon Chhota Nagra in person, walrus-moustached and radiating grievance, to inspect the district, the treasury, the lock-up, and you. He will form an opinion in the first ten minutes and spend the visit confirming it. The whole station has been whitewashed, including, it is rumoured, several things that were not walls.

choices.label: Show him a flawless, rehearsed district.
choices.outcome: Every ledger balances, every prisoner is suspiciously cheerful, every road has been mended along precisely the stretch he will drive. He leaves satisfied. The performance has cost you a fortnight and a small piece of your soul, both of which the Service considers a fair price.

choices.label: Show him the real district, warts and all.
choices.outcome: You show him the flooded quarter, the short revenue, the honest mess of the thing. He is appalled by your candour and, in a corner of his walrus heart he will never admit to, faintly impressed. It will not help your career. It may help you sleep.

choices.label: Ply him with the Club's best brandy and change the subject.
choices.outcome: By the second brandy he is telling you about his own first district; by the third, the inspection is effectively over. You have learned that the Empire, at its highest levels, runs substantially on the avoidance of awkwardness.

title: Fever in the Bazaar
body: A fever — the Civil Surgeon says cholera, the bazaar says worse — appears in the crowded lanes behind the grain market. The Surgeon wants the quarter cordoned and the wells closed. The traders want the market open. The pilgrims want to keep moving. Everyone wants you to choose, so that there will be someone to blame.

choices.label: Cordon the quarter and close the wells. Public health first.
choices.outcome: The fever is contained; the trade is throttled; the traders write to Simla about the high-handed young Magistrate. You saved lives and made enemies, and only one of those two things generates correspondence.

choices.label: Keep the market open and hope the Surgeon is exaggerating.
choices.outcome: The market thrives for eleven days. On the twelfth, the Surgeon is proved right in the way that surgeons are proved right, and the cordon you refused to order becomes a cordon you cannot make wide enough.

choices.label: Split the difference: cordon quietly, keep up appearances.
choices.outcome: You do half of what the Surgeon asked and claim to have done all of it and none of it, depending on the audience. The fever, indifferent to your positioning, does slightly less than its worst.

title: A Question of Precedence
body: At the Club's cold-weather ball, a furious dispute erupts over the order of precedence at dinner — specifically, whether the Executive Engineer's wife outranks the Forest Officer's wife. It is, everyone agrees, a trivial matter. It is also, everyone understands, a matter that could poison the entire station for a season.

choices.label: Rule strictly by the Warrant of Precedence.
choices.outcome: You produce the actual Warrant of Precedence, an object roughly as sacred here as scripture, and settle the matter by the book. Both wives are furious, but at the book, which cannot be invited to dinner or snubbed at it.

choices.label: Seat them apart and pretend it was always so.
choices.outcome: A little diplomatic fiction, gracefully deployed. The ball proceeds. You have discovered that the skills of a District Magistrate and the skills of a nervous head waiter are, at the Club, precisely identical.

choices.label: Declare you will not adjudicate the seating of a dinner.
choices.outcome: Principled, and a grave misreading of the room. At a frontier station the seating of a dinner is the government. By declining to rule, you have not risen above the station's politics; you have merely lost them.

title: The Case of the Stolen Buffalo
body: A cultivator stands accused of stealing his neighbour's buffalo. The evidence is a tangle of perjury on both sides, the village is split, and the truth — that the buffalo wandered and both men are lying about the rest — is not available in any form the law can use. Both families are watching your face for the verdict.

choices.label: Convict on the letter of the evidence.
choices.outcome: You convict the man the paperwork points to, who is probably guilty of something, if not this. The law is served. Justice files no return and is not consulted.

choices.label: Acquit for reasonable doubt and return the buffalo.
choices.outcome: You cut the knot: doubt to the accused, buffalo to its likely owner, a small homily to both families. Nobody is fully satisfied, which in a village dispute is the surest sign of a fair result.

choices.label: Bind both parties over and make them share the beast.
choices.outcome: Solomon in a solar topi. The two families are bound to joint custody of one bad-tempered buffalo, an arrangement so mutually inconvenient that they are reconciled by the shared grievance within the year.

title: The Camp at Rampur
body: Your tents are pitched under a mango tope outside Rampur; the patwari’s land-records are spread on the camp table, the headman is anxious, and a queue of cultivators has formed to lay grievances before the sahib in person. This is the district as it actually is, not as the files describe it.

choices.label: Go through the land records line by line with the patwari.
choices.outcome: You find three fields recorded to men who died in the last famine and one to a man who never existed. The patwari is either a rogue or an artist; either way the records are truer tonight than they were this morning.

choices.label: Hear the cultivators’ grievances under the mango tree.
choices.outcome: You sit until dark hearing of a bad well, a hard landlord, a boundary that has walked in the night. You can mend perhaps one grievance in five, but being heard by the sahib is itself a kind of remedy, and the village knows it.

choices.label: Keep it brief — show the flag and move on.
choices.outcome: You are seen, saluted, and gone by noon. The tour register records a village inspected. What the village records is that the sahib did not stay to listen.

title: The River Comes Up
body: Three days of rain and the river is over its banks; the low villages are islands, the rail embankment is the only high ground for miles, and a crowd of the flooded-out is gathering on it with their cattle and their cooking pots. Boats are few, the night is coming on, and the water is still rising.

choices.label: Take personal charge of the rescue from a boat.
choices.outcome: You spend two nights on the water pulling families off rooftops, soaked and sleepless and more use than you have felt in months. The district will long remember that the sahib came himself. So, unfortunately, will your constitution.

choices.label: Organise from the embankment — relief camp, grain, order.
choices.outcome: You set up the relief camp, commandeer the grain, and keep a frightened crowd from becoming a mob. Unglamorous, competent, and precisely the job. Nobody drowns who can be reached; some cannot be reached.

choices.label: Wire for military help and hold the line till it comes.
choices.outcome: The sappers arrive with boats on the second day and do the work you could not. It is the sensible call, and the district notes that in its worst hour the sahib sent a telegram and waited. Sense is rarely forgiven.

title: The Procession and the Mosque
body: The great autumn procession of one community is due to pass, as it has for a century, down the lane that runs past the other community's chief mosque at the hour of prayer. Both parties have come to your cutcherry — one citing custom, one citing insult — and both have brought enough young men to make plain that this is no longer only a question of a route.

choices.label: Order the procession to keep its ancient route.
choices.outcome: You uphold custom and brace for it. The procession passes; there is shoving, a thrown brick, a lathi-charge that stops just short of a headline. Custom is preserved, and everyone is now quite certain that next year will be worse.

choices.label: Divert the procession by a longer, quieter road.
choices.outcome: You reroute it in the name of peace. One community mutters that the sahib has broken a hundred years of right; the other says nothing, and remembers that the sahib can be moved. You have bought the peace of this year with the authority of the next.

choices.label: Summon both sides and broker a compromise yourself.
choices.outcome: You spend three exhausting days hammering out a route, a timing, and a face-saving fiction for each side. It holds. It is the hardest and least visible work there is, and the only kind that leaves a district quieter than you found it.

title: The Dacoits of the Ravines
body: A gang has come up out of the ravine country — three villages robbed, a moneylender's house burned, and a growing suspicion among the cultivators that the sahib's writ stops where the good roads do. The Superintendent wants a sweep; the villages want protection; the dacoits, by all accounts, want to become a legend.

choices.label: Lead an armed sweep of the ravines in person.
choices.outcome: You spend a fortnight in the saddle in bad country and the gang scatters — two taken, one shot, the rest gone across the border. The ravines are quiet, your constitution less so, and the legend, annoyingly, only grows.

choices.label: Work quietly through informers and moneylenders.
choices.outcome: Money changes hands in the dark and, in time, so does information. The gang is broken from within — cheaper and cleverer than a sweep, and winning no one any medals, least of all you.

choices.label: Post a reward and leave it to the police.
choices.outcome: You do the correct, distant thing. The poster is much admired; the dacoits are not caught; the ravine villages draw the obvious conclusion about how far the sahib will actually ride for them.

title: The District Budget
body: The annual estimates are due at the Secretariat, and the district's slender purse must be divided between the things that keep people alive, the things that keep people quiet, and the things that keep Simla content. Ram Autar lays three drafts before you, each balanced, each a small betrayal of the other two.

choices.label: Fund public works — wells, roads, a dispensary.
choices.outcome: You spend on the unglamorous things a district actually needs. The wells get dug, the people are quietly better off, and the Secretariat notes that your establishment charges creep above the provincial average. One of these facts will follow you; guess which.

choices.label: Economise and return a surplus to the province.
choices.outcome: You hand Simla a tidy surplus and your district a leaking tank and a shut dispensary. The Financial Secretary is delighted. Delight, in the Finance Department, is the highest form of life.

choices.label: Quietly strengthen the police lines.
choices.outcome: You put the money where it buys quiet rather than gratitude. The lock-up is mended, the constables paid on time, and the district grows a little safer and a little more watched. You tell yourself these are the same thing.

title: The Zamindar and the Tenants
body: The zamindar of Pipariya has enhanced his tenants' rents to a figure the land cannot bear, and the tenants — forty families, and the record on their side for once — have brought it to your court. The zamindar has brought his pleader, his account books, and a pointed reminder that men of property are the natural friends of Government.

choices.label: Rule for the tenants and roll back the rents.
choices.outcome: You cut the rents to what the fields will yield. Forty families bless the sahib; the zamindar writes to the Commissioner about the dangerous radicalism of the young magistrate, and encloses, he regrets, a list of his loyal services to the Crown.

choices.label: Rule for the zamindar — a contract is a contract.
choices.outcome: You uphold the letter of the lease. The revenue is secured, the men of property reassured, and forty families learn exactly where they stand in the order of the sahib's concerns. Some will remember it at the next Congress meeting.

choices.label: Send it to arbitration and split the difference.
choices.outcome: You appoint arbitrators and land on a rent that pinches everyone equally. Neither side is happy, the record is muddied past appeal, and the essential business of the Raj — the postponement of a reckoning — is once more served.

title: A School for Sonpur
body: On tour you are met at Sonpur by villagers who have, astonishingly, built a schoolhouse with their own hands and their own rupees, and now ask only that Government supply a master and his salary. It is precisely the self-help the annual report always praises, and precisely the recurring charge the Finance Department exists to prevent.

choices.label: Sanction the master and the salary at once.
choices.outcome: You sign the sanction on the spot, to the frank astonishment of the deputation, who had budgeted a year of petitions for it. Sonpur gets its school. It is the rarest official pleasure: a small good done quickly, before anyone can explain why it can't be.

choices.label: Forward it through channels with a warm note.
choices.outcome: You do it properly, which is to say slowly. The file begins its long pilgrimage through the Education Department. The schoolhouse waits, empty and swept, a small monument to the distance between a village and the Secretariat.

choices.label: Praise their spirit and make no promises.
choices.outcome: You give them a handsome speech about self-reliance and no master. They built a school on the strength of the sahib's justice; they will draw their own conclusions about the strength of the sahib's word.

title: The Boycott of Foreign Cloth
body: Bonfires of Manchester cloth are being lit in the bazaar, and the mill-agents and box-wallahs — loyal men, taxpayers, the backbone of the revenue — demand that you stop this seditious burning of perfectly good imported goods. The cloth is, inconveniently, the burners' own property.

choices.label: Ban the bonfires as a breach of the peace.
choices.outcome: You forbid the burnings and thereby confirm, for anyone who doubted it, that the Government of India regards the burning of a man's own shirt as a threat to the Empire. The box-wallahs are grateful. The nationalist press could not have scripted you better.

choices.label: Permit it — a man may burn his own cloth.
choices.outcome: You decline to defend Manchester from the citizens of Chhota Nagra. The bonfires burn out on their own, as bonfires do, and the mill-agents write to the Chamber of Commerce about the alarming sympathies of the local magistrate.

choices.label: Look the other way and buy some khadi yourself.
choices.outcome: You have a homespun coat quietly made and wear it on tour. It is comfortable, it is a small treason, and Ram Autar's face when he sees it is the nearest thing to open emotion he has shown all year.

title: A Scandal at the Club
body: In the dead of the hot weather, with tempers and thermometers both past bearing, young Pemberton of the Police has been discovered in a compromising arrangement involving another man's wife, a great deal of the Club's whisky, and a challenge shouted across the billiard room. As the senior civil officer present, the mess of it lands, inevitably, on you.

choices.label: Hush it up and send Pemberton on sudden leave.
choices.outcome: You engineer a discreet transfer and a story about his health, and the station agrees, as stations do, to have seen nothing. The appearances are saved. Somewhere under them, everyone knows exactly what happened, which is the ordinary condition of station life.

choices.label: Report it properly up the chain.
choices.outcome: You do the honest thing and put it on paper. Pemberton's career ends; the wronged husband is not mollified; and the station marks you down as a man who cannot be trusted to keep a thing quiet — the one unforgivable sin at a small mess.

choices.label: Bang heads together and settle it over brandy.
choices.outcome: You lock the three of them in the card-room and do not let them out until there is an apology, a handshake, and a shared understanding that the alternative is you. It works, at some cost to your evening and to your faith in the ruling race.

title: The Commissioner's Durbar
body: A grand durbar is to be held — the Commissioner presiding, the district's notables assembled by rank, robes of honour distributed, loyalty affirmed, and the whole elaborate theatre of the Raj staged for an afternoon in the maidan. Your task is the seating: a chair too high or too low, a name called out of order, and a feud is born that will outlive you.

choices.label: Stage it flawlessly by the Warrant and the old lists.
choices.outcome: Every notable is seated to the inch of his dignity, every robe bestowed on cue, and the durbar unfolds like clockwork wound by a nervous man. The Commissioner is pleased; the notables placated; you have spent a week of your life on a seating plan and would, appallingly, do it again.

choices.label: Use the seating to reward the loyal, cool the awkward.
choices.outcome: You quietly promote the friends of Government up the rows and let the difficult men feel the draught from the back. It is deftly done and widely understood, and you have turned an afternoon of pageantry into a small, sharp instrument of rule. The Pandit, uninvited, is said to have laughed.

choices.label: Keep it plain and spend the saving on the district.
choices.outcome: You stage a modest durbar and divert the saved expense to a relief fund. The notables are faintly insulted to be honoured on a budget; the district notices that the sahib would rather feed it than flatter it. Only one of those constituencies writes the confidential reports.
